build.natural: the primes, $1$ and the composites make up $\mathbb{N}$.

about.natural: $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ is made of the primes $\mathbb{P}=\{2,3,5,7,\dots\}$, the number $1$ and the composites $\mathbb{K}=\{4,6,8,9,\dots\}$.
about.rational: $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ plus fractions such as $\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac23$. Every rational number can be written as $\tfrac{m}{n}$ with $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $n\neq 0$.
about.real: $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ plus the irrational numbers $\mathbb{I}_r$, such as $\sqrt2$, $e$ and $\pi$. Its line is whole, with no gaps.
about.complex: $\mathbb{C}=\{a+bi\mid a,b\in\mathbb{R},\ i^2=-1\}$. A real number is a complex number with $b=0$, for example $3=3+0i$, so it sits on the line. What gets added: the numbers with $b\neq 0$, off the line.

reasons.one: $1$ is neither prime nor composite, so it has its own part of $\mathbb{N}$.
reasons.two: $2$ is divisible only by $1$ and $2$: a prime.
reasons.three: $3$ is divisible only by $1$ and $3$: a prime.
reasons.zero: $0$ is not a natural number. It first appears in $\mathbb{C}_a$.
reasons.negative: a negative integer, which first appears in $\mathbb{Z}$.
reasons.fraction: a fraction that is not an integer, which first appears in $\mathbb{Q}$.
reasons.sqrtTwo: $\sqrt2$ cannot be written as $\tfrac{m}{n}$: an irrational number. In the $\mathbb{Q}$ row its place is still a gap.
reasons.pi: $\pi=3.14159\dots$ has decimals that never stop and never repeat: an irrational number. In the $\mathbb{Q}$ row its place is still a gap.
reasons.imaginaryUnit: $i=0+1i$, so $a=0$ and $b=1$. Since $b\neq 0$, the point leaves the real line, $1$ unit up.
reasons.onePlusTwoI: $a=1$ and $b=2$: $1$ unit right, $2$ units up. Since $b\neq 0$, it is not a real number.
reasons.sixThirds: looks like a fraction, but $6\div 3=2$: a prime.
reasons.sqrtNine: has a root sign, but $3\times 3=9$, so $\sqrt9=3$: a prime.
reasons.minusEightQuarters: $-8\div 4=-2$: a negative integer, not a fraction.
reasons.iSquared: has an $i$, but $i^2=-1$ by definition: a negative integer.
reasons.threeQuarters: a terminating decimal: $0.75=\tfrac{75}{100}=\tfrac34$, so it is rational.
reasons.repeating: a repeating decimal is rational too: let $x=0.333\dots$, then $10x-x=3$, so $x=\tfrac13$.
reasons.sqrtEight: $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$, and $\sqrt2$ is irrational, so $\sqrt8$ is irrational too.
reasons.sqrtMinusFour: no real number squares to $-4$. $\sqrt{-4}=2i$, because $(2i)^2=4i^2=-4$.

complexNumbers.title: Complex Numbers

plot.intro: a complex number $z = a + bi$ is drawn as the point $(a, b)$: the real part $a$ on the horizontal axis $\mathrm{Re}(z)$, the imaginary part $b$ on the vertical axis $\mathrm{Im}(z)$.
plot.summary: every $z = a + bi$ has exactly one point $(a, b)$ in the plane, and every point has exactly one $z$.
plot.hint: click a point, or play to draw them one by one.
captions: $z_1 = 1 + 2i$: 1 to the right along $\mathrm{Re}(z)$, then 2 up. The point is $(1, 2)$.
$z_2 = -2 + i$: 2 to the left, then 1 up. The point is $(-2, 1)$.
$z_3 = -1 - 2i$: 1 to the left, then 2 down. The point is $(-1, -2)$.
$z_4 = 2 - i$: 2 to the right, then 1 down. The point is $(2, -1)$.

add.intro: real adds to real, imaginary to imaginary. In the plane: start at $z_1$, then walk as far as $z_2$.
add.summary: $z_1 + z_2 = 3 - i$. Adding means joining: the walk of $z_2$ (2 right, 3 down) is attached to the end of $z_1$.
add.hint: click a point, or play to add part by part.
captions: real part: $1 + 2 = 3$. From $z_1$ move 2 to the right.
imaginary part: $2 + (-3) = -1$. Move 3 down.

subtract.intro: real minus real, imaginary minus imaginary. In the plane: start at $z_1$, then walk as far as $z_2$ in the opposite direction.
subtract.summary: $z_1 - z_2 = -1 + 5i$. Subtracting $z_2$ is walking as far as $z_2$ the other way: 2 left, 3 up.
subtract.hint: click a point, or play to subtract part by part.
captions: real part: $1 - 2 = -1$. From $z_1$ move 2 to the left.
imaginary part: $2 - (-3) = 5$. Move 3 up.

multiply.intro: every term times every term, like $(a + b)(c + d)$. The difference: $i \cdot i = i^2 = -1$, so imaginary times imaginary moves to the real part.
multiply.summary: $z_1 \cdot z_2 = 8 + i$. The term $2i \cdot (-3i)$ looks imaginary, but $i^2 = -1$ makes it real: 6 to the right, not up.
multiply.hint: click a point, or play to fill the boxes one by one.
captions: $1 \cdot 2 = 2$, real. From 0 move 2 to the right.
$1 \cdot (-3i) = -3i$, imaginary. Move 3 down, right onto $z_2$, because $1 \cdot z_2 = z_2$.
$2i \cdot 2 = 4i$, imaginary. Move 4 up.
$2i \cdot (-3i) = -6i^2 = 6$, because $i^2 = -1$. So it is real: move 6 to the right.
real $2 + 6 = 8$, imaginary $-3i + 4i = i$. So $z_1 \cdot z_2 = 8 + i$.

divide.intro: multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, $\bar{z}_2$. The bottom becomes a real number, then each part is simply divided.
divide.hint: click a point, or play to divide step by step.
captions: conjugate of the bottom: $\bar{z}_2 = 2 + 3i$, the mirror of $z_2$ in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
bottom: $(2 - 3i)(2 + 3i) = 4 + 9 = 13$. The imaginary part cancels, so it is real.
divide by 13: $\tfrac{z_1}{z_2} = -\tfrac{4}{13} + \tfrac{7}{13}i$. Same direction as $-4 + 7i$, 13 times closer to 0.

conjugate.intro: the conjugate of $z = a + bi$ is $\bar{z} = a - bi$: the imaginary part changes sign. In the plane: a mirror in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
conjugate.summary: conjugate = mirror in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis. That is why $\overline{z_1 - z_2} = \bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2$: both are the point $(-1, -5)$.
conjugate.hint: click a point, or play to mirror them one by one.
captions: $\bar{z}_1 = 1 - 2i$: the mirror of $z_1$ in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
$\bar{z}_2 = 2 + 3i$: the mirror of $z_2$.
$z_1 - z_2 = -1 + 5i$, as on the $z_1 - z_2$ tab.
the mirror of $z_1 - z_2$ lands on the same point: $\overline{z_1 - z_2} = \bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2$.

readings: $P$ = T, $Q$ = T: graduated and in good health, like Amir. Both requirements are met, so $P \wedge Q$ = T: accepted.
$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: graduated but not in good health. One requirement fails, so $P \wedge Q$ = F: not accepted.

$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: did not graduate and not in good health. Both requirements fail, so $P \wedge Q$ = F: not accepted.
conjunction.definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two propositions. The conjunction of $P$ and $Q$, written $P \wedge Q$, is true if both are true, and false otherwise.

suppose: $P \vee Q$: Amir goes to Bandung *or* Amad goes to Bandung

$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: only Amir goes. One true part is enough, so $P \vee Q$ = T.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = T: only Amad goes. One true part is enough, so $P \vee Q$ = T.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: nobody goes to Bandung. Both are false, so $P \vee Q$ = F.

commutativeAdd.title: commutative addition
commutativeAdd.intro: Commutative means the order can be swapped. Forward 2 then 3, or forward 3 then 2, both stop at 5.
steps: Left side $2 + 3$: start at 0, move forward 2 to 2.
Forward 3 more, stop at 5. So $2 + 3 = 5$.
Right side $3 + 2$: start at 0, move forward 3 to 3.
Forward 2 more, stop at 5. So $3 + 2 = 5$.
Both sides stop at 5, so $2 + 3 = 3 + 2$.

commutativeMul.title: commutative multiplication
commutativeMul.intro: Swapping the order of a product mirrors its rectangle in the diagonal. The number of squares does not change.
steps: Left side $2 \cdot (-4)$: across 2 to the right, down 4. It holds 8 squares in a negative region, so $-8$.
Right side $(-4) \cdot 2$: across 4 to the left, up 2. It also holds 8 squares in a negative region, so $-8$.
Mirrored in the diagonal, the two rectangles swap places. Still 8 squares, still negative, so $2 \cdot (-4) = (-4) \cdot 2$.

associativeAdd.title: associative addition
associativeAdd.intro: Associative means the grouping can move. The brackets decide which jumps are joined first, but the end point stays the same.
steps: Left side $2 + (4 + \tfrac{1}{2})$: forward 2 to 2.
Brackets first: $4 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 4\tfrac{1}{2}$, one jump from 2 to $6\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Right side $(2 + 4) + \tfrac{1}{2}$: brackets first, $2 + 4 = 6$, one jump to 6.
Forward $\tfrac{1}{2}$ more, stop at $6\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Both sides stop at $6\tfrac{1}{2}$. The brackets moved, the result did not.

associativeMul.title: associative multiplication
associativeMul.intro: Three factors build a cuboid. Cut it flat into layers or upright into slices, the number of cubes stays the same.
steps: Left side $2\big((3)(4)\big)$: brackets first, $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ cubes in one layer.
Two layers: $2 \cdot 12 = 24$ cubes.
Right side $\big((2)(3)\big)4$: brackets first, $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ cubes in one slice.
Four slices: $6 \cdot 4 = 24$ cubes.
The same $2 \times 3 \times 4$ cuboid, only cut in a different way. Both sides are 24.

distributive.title: distributive
distributive.intro: Distributivity links multiplication with addition: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ multiplies every term inside the brackets.
steps: Left side $\tfrac{1}{2}(2 + 4)$: brackets first, $2 + 4 = 6$.
A $\tfrac{1}{2}$ by 6 rectangle: six half squares, area 3.
Right side: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2) = 1$, two half squares.
Both sides are 3. Cutting a rectangle in two does not change its area.

identityAdd.title: additive identity
identityAdd.intro: The identity for addition is 0: adding 0 does not move the point.
steps: Left side $-4 + 0$: move back 4 to $-4$.
Add 0: no move at all, still at $-4$.
Right side $-4$: move back 4 to $-4$.
Both sides are at $-4$. Adding 0 leaves the number unchanged.

identityMul.title: multiplicative identity
identityMul.intro: The identity for multiplication is 1: a rectangle of height 1 has an area equal to its length.
steps: Left side $(4)(1)$: a 4 by 1 rectangle, 4 squares.
Right side 4: length 4 on the number line.
Height 1 makes the area equal to the length, so $(4)(1) = 4$.

inverseAdd.title: additive inverse
inverseAdd.intro: The additive inverse of 6 is $-6$: forward 6, then back 6, home at 0.
steps: Left side $6 + (-6)$: forward 6 to 6.
Add $-6$: back 6, home at 0.
Right side 0: stay at 0.
Both sides are at 0. $-6$ is the additive inverse of 6.

inverseMul.title: multiplicative inverse
inverseMul.intro: The multiplicative inverse of 2 is $2^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}$: a 2 by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ rectangle is exactly one square.
steps: Left side $2 \cdot 2^{-1}$ with $2^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}$: a 2 by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ rectangle, two half squares.
Right side 1: one whole square.
Two half squares stacked make one square, so $2 \cdot 2^{-1} = 1$.

subtraction.title: subtraction
subtraction.intro: Subtraction is not a new operation: $4 - 3$ means 4 plus the inverse of 3, which is $-3$.
steps: Left side $4 - 3$ is read as $4 + (-3)$. Forward 4 to 4.
Add $-3$, the inverse of 3: back 3 to 1.
Right side 1: forward 1 to 1.
Both sides are at 1, so $4 - 3 = 4 + (-3) = 1$.

division.title: division
division.intro: Division is not a new operation: $\tfrac{4}{2}$ means 4 times the inverse of 2, which is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
steps: Left side $\tfrac{4}{2}$ is read as $4 \cdot 2^{-1} = 4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}$: a 4 by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ rectangle, four half squares.
Right side 2: two whole squares.
Four half squares make two squares, so $\tfrac{4}{2} = 4 \cdot 2^{-1} = 2$.

otherRemarks.distributive: both sides are 16. 6 − 2 is read as 6 + (−2), so 4 multiplies both 6 and −2.

steps: $x = -5$ is left of $y = 3$. Only $x < y$ is true.
$x = 3$ is on $y = 3$. Only $x = y$ is true.
$x = 8$ is right of $y = 3$. Only $x > y$ is true.
$x = -6$ is left of 0, so $x < 0$: $x$ is negative.
$x = 0$ is on 0: neither positive nor negative.
$x = 4$ is right of 0, so $x > 0$: $x$ is positive.
$x = 3$ is left of $y = 7$, so $3 < 7$.
$y = 7$ is left of $z = 9$, so $7 < 9$.
Two steps to the right together still go right: $x$ is left of $z$, so $3 < 9$.
$x = -2$ is left of $y = 3$, so $-2 < 3$.
$y = 3$ is left of $z = 9$, so $3 < 9$.
Two steps to the right together still go right: $x$ is left of $z$, so $-2 < 9$.
Start from $x = 3$ and $y = 7$: $3$ is left of $7$, so $3 < 7$.
$\Rightarrow$ Add $z = 9$ to both sides. Both points move 9 to the right: $12 < 16$, the order stays.
$\Leftarrow$ Add $-9$ to both sides. Both points move 9 to the left, back to $3 < 7$.
With $z = -5$ both points move left: $-2 < 2$. The order stays too.
$z = 3 > 0$: $xz = 6$ and $yz = 12$. The connecting lines do not cross, $6 < 12$. The sign stays.
$z = -3 < 0$: $xz = -6$ and $yz = -12$. The connecting lines cross above 0, $-6 > -12$. The sign flips.
$z = -\tfrac{1}{2} < 0$: $xz = -1$ and $yz = -2$. They cross again, $-1 > -2$.
$z = \tfrac{1}{2} > 0$: $xz = 1$ and $yz = 2$. The line shrinks toward 0 without crossing, $1 < 2$.

intros.trichotomyY: Two numbers $x$ and $y$ have only three possible positions on the number line: $x$ left of $y$, on $y$, or right of $y$. Exactly one happens, so exactly one of $x < y$, $x = y$, $x > y$ is true.
intros.trichotomyZero: The number 0 splits $\mathbb{R}$ into two parts. Numbers right of 0 are positive, numbers left of 0 are negative. 0 itself is neither.
intros.transitive: If $x$ is left of $y$ and $y$ is left of $z$, then $x$ must be left of $z$. Two steps to the right together are still one step to the right.
intros.addition: Adding $z$ to both sides moves both points by $z$ in the same direction. Their order and distance stay the same, for positive and negative $z$ alike. The sign $\iff$ means it works both ways: add $z$, then add $-z$ to go back.
intros.multiplication: Multiplying by $z > 0$ stretches or shrinks the line from 0, the order stays. Multiplying by $z < 0$ also flips the line at 0: what was on the left moves to the right. That is why the order sign flips.

inequalities.title: Inequalities
inequalities.idle: press start to see the steps one by one, or move $x$ to test it.

steps: The equation $x - 2 = 0$.
Add 2 to both sides: $x = 2$.
Only one point satisfies it: $\{2\}$.
The equation $x^2 - \tfrac{1}{4} = 0$.
Factor the left side: $(x - \tfrac{1}{2})(x + \tfrac{1}{2}) = 0$.
A product is 0 when one of its factors is 0: $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$ or $x = -\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Two points satisfy it: $\{-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\}$.
The inequality $x < 1$.
Every point left of 1 satisfies it, 1 itself does not: the interval $(-\infty, 1)$.
Start from $2x - 4 < 0$.
Add 4 to both sides (addition axiom).
Simplify: $2x < 4$.
Divide both sides by 2. Since $2 > 0$, the sign stays: $x < 2$.
So every $x$ left of 2 satisfies it, 2 itself does not: the interval $(-\infty, 2)$.
Start from $-2x + 4 < 0$.
Add $-4$ to both sides.
Simplify: $-2x < -4$.
Divide both sides by $-2$. Since $-2 < 0$, the sign flips: $x > 2$.
So every $x$ right of 2 satisfies it: the interval $(2, \infty)$.
Start from $0 < 2x - 2 \le 4$. It has three parts.
Add 2 to every part.
Simplify: $2 < 2x \le 6$.
Divide every part by 2 (multiply by $2^{-1}$), the sign stays: $1 < x \le 3$.
So $x$ lies between 1 and 3, without 1 but with 3: the interval $(1, 3]$.
Start from $10 \ge 2x + 6 \ge 4$.
Subtract 6 from every part: $4 \ge 2x \ge -2$.
Divide every part by 2: $2 \ge x \ge -1$.
Read it from right to left, it means the same: $-1 \le x \le 2$.
So $x$ runs from $-1$ to 2, both ends included: the interval $[-1, 2]$.
Start from $5x + 6 < 3x + 14$. There is an $x$ on both sides.
Add $(-3x - 6)$ to both sides, so the $x$ terms gather on the left and the numbers on the right.
Simplify: $2x < 8$.
Divide both sides by 2, the sign stays: $x < 4$.
So the interval is $(-\infty, 4)$.
Start from $-2x + 10 \ge 3x - 5$.
Add $(-3x - 10)$ to both sides.
Simplify: $-5x \ge -15$.
Divide by $-5$ (multiply by $-\tfrac{1}{5}$). It is negative, so the sign flips: $x \le 3$.
So the interval is $(-\infty, 3]$, with 3 included.

intros.compare: An equation is satisfied by a few points, finitely many. An inequality is satisfied by a whole interval, infinitely many.
intros.linear: Inequalities are solved with the order axioms: add the same number to both sides, then divide by the coefficient of $x$. If the coefficient is negative, the order sign flips.
intros.chained: A chained inequality has three parts. Every step is applied to all three parts at once.
intros.bothSides: If $x$ appears on both sides, first gather the $x$ terms on one side by adding their opposites to both sides.

steps: The equation $\lvert 4x + 3 \rvert = 7$: the inside of the absolute value is 7 away from 0.
By Definition 4.2.1, the inside is 7 or $-7$.
Subtract 3 from both sides of each part.
Divide by 4: $x = 1$ or $x = -\tfrac{10}{4}$.
Two points satisfy it: $\{-\tfrac{10}{4}, 1\}$.
The equation $\lvert 7x \rvert = x - 4$. Its right side contains $x$.
Open the absolute value as in the first example.
Gather the $x$ terms: $6x = -4$ or $8x = 4$.
Divide: the candidates are $x = -\tfrac{4}{6}$ or $x = \tfrac{4}{8}$.
But $\lvert 7x \rvert$ is never negative, so neither is the right side: $x - 4 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge 4$.
Both candidates are less than 4, so both are rejected. No $x$ satisfies it: $\varnothing$.
The equation $\lvert 5x - 3 \rvert = \lvert 3x + 5 \rvert$: both insides are equally far from 0.
Two numbers are equally far from 0 when they are equal or opposite.
Gather the $x$ terms on the left and the numbers on the right.
Divide: $x = 4$ or $x = -\tfrac{2}{8}$.
Two points satisfy it: $\{-\tfrac{2}{8}, 4\}$.
$\lvert x \rvert < 3$: the distance from $x$ to 0 is less than 3.
Points closer than 3 to 0 lie between $-3$ and 3.
The ends $-3$ and 3 are exactly 3 away, so they are not included: the interval $(-3, 3)$.
$\lvert x \rvert > 3$: the distance from $x$ to 0 is more than 3.
The points lie left of $-3$ or right of 3.
Two parts, ends not included: $(-\infty, -3) \cup (3, \infty)$.
$\lvert x \rvert \le 3$: the distance from $x$ to 0 is at most 3.
The points lie between $-3$ and 3, both included.
The ends are exactly 3 away and $3 \le 3$, so they are included: the interval $[-3, 3]$.
$\lvert x \rvert \ge 3$: the distance from $x$ to 0 is at least 3.
The points lie left of $-3$ or right of 3, both included.
Two parts, ends included: $(-\infty, -3] \cup [3, \infty)$.
Start from $\lvert x - 4 \rvert < 7$.
Theorem 4.2.1(a) with $x - 4$ in place of $x$ and $a = 7$.
Add 4 to every part.
Simplify: $-3 < x < 11$.
So the interval is $(-3, 11)$.
Start from $\lvert 2x - 5 \rvert < 3$.
Add 5 to every part: $2 < 2x < 8$.
Divide every part by 2: $1 < x < 4$.
So the interval is $(1, 4)$.
Start from $\lvert x - 3 \rvert > 5$.
Theorem 4.2.1(b): two parts joined by or.
Add 3 to both sides of each part: $x < -2$ or $x > 8$.
So two intervals: $(-\infty, -2) \cup (8, \infty)$.
Start from $\lvert 3x - 7 \rvert > 2$.
Divide by 3: $x < \tfrac{5}{3}$ or $x > 3$.
So $(-\infty, \tfrac{5}{3}) \cup (3, \infty)$.
Start from $\lvert 3x - 2 \rvert \le 4$.
Corollary 4.2.1(a): $-4 \le 3x - 2 \le 4$.
Add 2 to every part: $-2 \le 3x \le 6$.
Divide every part by 3: $-\tfrac{2}{3} \le x \le 2$.
So the interval is $[-\tfrac{2}{3}, 2]$, both ends included.
Start from $\lvert 3x - 4 \rvert \ge 2$.
Corollary 4.2.1(b): $3x - 4 \le -2$ or $3x - 4 \ge 2$.
Add 4: $3x \le 2$ or $3x \ge 6$.
Divide by 3: $x \le \tfrac{2}{3}$ or $x \ge 2$.
So $(-\infty, \tfrac{2}{3}] \cup [2, \infty)$, ends included.

intros.reflexive: A relation on $A$ is reflexive if every member is related to itself: $a \mathrel{\mathrm R} a$ for every $a \in A$. Check the members one by one.

properties.footnote: A partial order needs three properties. A total order also needs every two members to be comparable.

loops.name: loops
loops.why: every member is related to itself (reflexive), so the loops carry no information

shortcuts.name: shortcuts
shortcuts.why: if $a \to b \to c$ is there, transitivity gives $a \to c$ for free

arrows.name: arrowheads
arrows.why: smaller members are drawn lower, so every line is read upward

linesCard.count: {{count}} lines remain: the pairs where nothing lies in between. Left out: {{loops}} loops and {{shortcuts}} shortcuts.

membersCard.footnote: A least member is always the only minimal one. The other way round fails: with two minimal members, neither is the least. Click a member in the diagram to highlight its row.

formulas.antisymmetric: a \preceq b \land b \preceq a \Rightarrow a = b
formulas.transitive: a \preceq b \land b \preceq c \Rightarrow a \preceq c
formulas.total: \forall a, b:\ a \preceq b \lor b \preceq a
formulas.cover: a \prec b \text{ with no } c \text{ such that } a \prec c \prec b

rules.total: total order (linear order): every two members are comparable
rules.cover: a line in the Hasse diagram: $b$ lies directly above $a$

orderRelations.rulesFootnote: $\preceq$ is the usual sign for a partial order: $a \preceq b$ means $a \mathrel{\mathrm R} b$. $a \prec b$ means $a \preceq b$ and $a \ne b$.

intros.partial: A relation on $A$ that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive is a partial order, often written $\preceq$. If moreover every two members can be compared, it is a total order.
intros.hasse: A Hasse diagram is a tidy picture of a partial order: smaller members lower, and only the lines between neighbours. Everything else follows from the properties.
intros.extremes: A minimal member has nothing below it; a least member lies below everything. In a total order they are the same, in a partial order they are not.

tips.partial: $\le$ is a total order, $\mid$ (divides) only a partial order: 2 and 3 do not divide each other.
tips.hasse: Compare the divisors of 30 with the subsets of $\{a, b, c\}$: the two Hasse diagrams have the same shape.
tips.extremes: Try $\{2, 3, 4, 6\}$: two minimal and two maximal members, but no least and no greatest.
